recent_posts.title: When Your Hash Becomes a String: Hunting Ruby’s Million-to-One Memory Bug
recent_posts.summary: A deep technical investigation into a rare Ruby bug where FFI structs' internal Hashes were being freed by the garbage collector and replaced by Strings at the same memory address. The bug, caused by missing write barriers in FFI versions before 1.17.0, occurred roughly once per million process restarts but cascaded into thousands of errors when triggered. The author methodically ruled out musl libc issues, struct alignment problems, and ABI mismatches before discovering the root cause: FFI's C extension wasn't properly registering object references with Ruby's GC, allowing use-after-free conditions where objects could transform into completely different types at runtime.

recent_posts.title: Announcing llm-docs-builder: An Open Source Tool for Making Documentation AI-Friendly
recent_posts.summary: llm-docs-builder is an open-source tool that transforms Markdown documentation into AI-optimized formats, reducing token usage by 85-95% compared to HTML versions. It strips noise like CSS, JavaScript, and HTML boilerplate while preserving semantic structure and context hierarchy. The tool generates llms.txt indexes for AI discoverability and can be configured to automatically serve optimized markdown to AI crawlers while maintaining HTML for human visitors. Real-world metrics from Karafka framework show 20-36x file size reductions, translating to lower RAG costs and fewer hallucinations.

recent_posts.title: WaterDrop Meets Ruby’s Async Ecosystem: Lightweight Concurrency Done Right
recent_posts.summary: WaterDrop 2.8.7 introduces transparent async support using Ruby's fiber-based concurrency, delivering up to 5x throughput improvements for Kafka operations without requiring code changes. The integration leverages the async gem's lightweight fibers to automatically yield during I/O operations, enabling concurrent message production while maintaining Ruby's familiar programming model. Benchmarks show significant performance gains over traditional sequential processing and threading approaches.

recent_posts.title: From pidfd to Shimanami Kaido: My RubyKaigi 2025 Experience
recent_posts.summary: The post describes the author's experience at RubyKaigi 2025, the largest Ruby conference, held in Matsuyama, Japan. It highlights how RubyKaigi uniquely bridges the Japanese and Western Ruby communities, the enriching talks and discussions on topics like ZJIT and Ractor-local GC, and the meaningful interactions beyond the official event schedule. The author also shares post-conference adventures, such as cycling the Shimanami Kaido, emphasizing the conference's role in fostering international connections and unique cultural experiences.

recent_posts.title: Fixing expired certificate issue on your Chromecast
recent_posts.summary: On March 9, 2025, many Chromecast 2nd generation and Chromecast Audio devices stopped working due to an expired device authentication certificate. This guide provides temporary workarounds for both non-reset and factory-reset Chromecast devices until Google releases an official fix. Users are cautioned about security risks and advised to proceed at their own risk.

recent_posts.title: Breaking the Rules: RPC Pattern with Apache Kafka and Karafka
recent_posts.summary: Implementing RPC patterns with Apache Kafka using Karafka can be controversial due to Kafka's design focused on event logging and throughput. This proof-of-concept approach achieves millisecond response times under ideal conditions by leveraging synchronous RPC-like behavior over Kafka's asynchronous nature. While this pattern may not be production-ready, it provides valuable insights into extending existing infrastructure without adding complexity. Careful attention to timeouts, error handling, and monitoring is required for success.

recent_posts.title: The Silent Guardian: Why Bundler Checksums Are a Game-Changer for Your Applications
recent_posts.summary: Bundler 2.6 introduces a new checksum verification feature to ensure the integrity of Ruby gems throughout the software supply chain. This mechanism protects against tampering by verifying that gems have not been altered since they were first recorded. It offers automated protection during installation and builds trust in the Ruby ecosystem. While it can't prevent the release of new malicious gems, it guards against replacement attacks, ensuring developers use untampered dependencies.

recent_posts.title: Under the Hood: Enhancing Karafka’s CPU and Memory Efficiency
recent_posts.summary: The post discusses recent performance enhancements in Karafka, focusing on CPU and memory efficiency. Several pull requests were made to reduce memory allocation and improve time tracking management. Specific changes include optimizing instrumentation data handling, avoiding unnecessary event measurements when no listeners are present, and refining time measurement techniques to reduce object creation and improve execution speed. These updates aim to deliver top-notch data-streaming tools for the Ruby community.

recent_posts.title: The librdkafka Supply Chain Breakdown: rdkafka-ruby’s Darkest Hour
recent_posts.summary: The `rdkafka-ruby` gem faced significant installation issues when the `librdkafka` repository on GitHub went private. This disruption highlighted the risks of relying on external resources and the importance of immutable builds. Plans to internalize `librdkafka` in future releases are underway to ensure stability and reliability. The incident underscores the fragility of the OSS supply chain and the need for better design and dependency management practices.

recent_posts.title: From Sleep to Speed: Making Rdkafka Sync Operations 16 Times Faster
recent_posts.summary: This post discusses how replacing sleep with condition variables and mutexes improved the performance of rdkafka by eliminating unnecessary wait times, optimizing resource usage, and aligning better with Ruby's scheduling model.
